case_study_insert.main_stem: Golden Gate Leisure (GGL) is a private limited company in the leisure and entertainment sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 1988 by Priya Raman, it runs an indoor entertainment complex with arcades and a food court, and combines democratic leadership with a hierarchical structure. GGL plans to invest $1,500,000 in a new gaming and dining floor, financed by a $900,000 ten-year bank loan and $600,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $1,800,000 a year, a variable cost of $35 per guest visit and a selling price of $95 per guest visit, and currently produces 55,000 units a year. GGL faces two problems: food waste is rising and cleanliness complaints have increased.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report, Q4 2025: GGL logged 13,500 guest visits last quarter, with a food-waste rate of 7.8%, up from 5.2% a year earlier. Cleanliness complaint cards rose from 44 to 63 per month and the quality circle recorded 51 defective arcade-machine service calls. Average table clearance time was 22 minutes. A survey of 800 visitors found 66% would pay $8 more for a cleaner venue and 53% consider waste reduction important. Recycling training costs $320 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Golden Gate Leisure as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Leisure Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, raising borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $12.40 to $13.12 per hour from April 2026. (3) Food and beverage input costs have risen 10.1% year-on-year, while consumer spending on leisure grew only 2.9% and inflation is 6.6%.

questions.question_text: GGL plans to finance part of its $1,500,000 expansion with retained profit. Explain two advantages for GGL of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit of $600,000 needs no interest or capital repayment, unlike the $900,000 ten-year bank loan whose cost rises with the base rate now at 4.75%. With $1,800,000 fixed costs and a food-waste rate of 7.8%, avoiding interest protects the $60 contribution per guest visit and leaves more cash to tackle the 63 monthly cleanliness complaints without raising the $95 price. With 63 complaints a month, protecting quality spending matters more than avoiding interest.

Point 2: Internal funding keeps decision-making with the existing owners and avoids pledging GGL's $4,700,000 of non-current assets as loan collateral. It is also quick: the new dining floor can open without waiting for lender approval, which matters while consumer spending on leisure grows only 2.9% and food and beverage inputs cost 10.1% more — early opening captures demand before conditions tighten further, helping GGL take a share of the limited 2.9% growth in leisure spending.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to GGL's expansion and financing.

questions.question_text: GGL wants to attract visitors to its new dining floor. Consider newspaper coupons, a loyalty card scheme, or influencer launch events. Which should GGL choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Newspaper coupons: Coupons can stimulate trial of the new dining floor and are simple to distribute locally. However, print reach is falling and coupons train guests to wait for discounts, which would cut the $95 selling price and the $60 contribution needed to justify a $1,500,000 investment. Response is hard to track, so GGL cannot tell whether the 13,500 guest visits actually rise.

Loyalty card scheme: A loyalty card rewards repeat visits and lets GGL record which guests return, directly targeting the 66% of 800 surveyed visitors who would pay $8 more for a cleaner venue and the 53% who value waste reduction. It builds a customer database for future offers and suits a 120-strong entertainment complex with many repeat local guests. The drawback is the cost of rewards and administration, and it mainly affects existing customers rather than attracting new ones.

Influencer launch events: Inviting lifestyle influencers could generate buzz about the new floor and reach younger visitors quickly. Yet the impact may be short-lived, fees are unpredictable, and the 2.9% growth in leisure spending means only limited discretionary budgets to capture, so the spend may not convert into enough $95 visits.

Recommendation: GGL should choose the loyalty card scheme. It encourages repeat $95 visits, gathers data, and reinforces the cleanliness and waste message that matters to 66% and 53% of respondents. Coupons are rejected because they erode the $60 contribution, and influencer events because their buzz is brief and costly; loyalty gives measurable, lasting revenue to service the $900,000 loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to GGL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in GGL's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in GGL's context with a justified recommendation explaining why coupons and influencer events are rejected.

questions.question_text: GGL's food waste has reached 7.8% and cleanliness complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for GGL of its democratic leadership style.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership lets the 120 staff propose practical ways to cut the 7.8% waste rate, such as portion control in the food court, and the quality circle can turn those ideas into action. Because staff serve guests daily, their suggestions are practical and can reduce waste from 7.8% toward the 5.2% level of a year ago, protecting the $60 contribution per visit by lowering the $35 variable cost as waste falls toward 5.2%.

Point 2: Involving employees in decisions raises ownership of cleanliness, which can cut the 63 monthly complaint cards and support the 66% of surveyed visitors who would pay $8 more for a cleaner venue. Higher involvement also improves motivation in a hierarchical structure and makes the $320 recycling training more effective, as staff apply what they learn rather than resent it. Across a complex with 120 staff, that involvement is hard for managers to achieve alone.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to GGL's waste, complaints and staff.

questions.question_text: GGL must reduce its 7.8% food-waste rate. Consider quality control inspections or quality assurance through staff training. Which should GGL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Quality control inspections: Checking food and cleaning standards at the end of service can catch faults before guests see them, cutting the 63 monthly complaints and the 51 defective arcade-machine calls. It gives measurable results quickly and suits a hierarchical structure. However, inspection finds errors only after resources are wasted, takes staff time, and does not by itself reduce the 7.8% waste rate, while the $900,000 loan limits extra supervision costs, and the 22-minute table clearance time shows how delays build at peak periods.

Quality assurance through training: Teaching all 120 staff to prevent waste and clean correctly attacks the cause of the 7.8% rate rather than the symptoms, aiming to return toward 5.2%. The $320 per-employee recycling training is a modest cost, it builds a culture of prevention, and democratic leadership supports staff input through the quality circle. The limits are that results take time and training must be refreshed as staff turn over. Prevention suits democratic leadership because staff propose their own waste-saving ideas.

Decision: GGL should choose quality assurance through training, with light inspections as a check. Prevention fits the 53% of surveyed visitors who value waste reduction, reduces the waste that erodes the $60 contribution, and is affordable at $320 per employee. Pure inspection is rejected because it detects waste only after it occurs and cannot deliver the lasting fall from 7.8% needed to protect the $1,500,000 investment. With $1,800,000 fixed costs, avoiding waste is cheaper than inspecting it after the event. Cleaner venues support the 66% who would pay $8 more.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two approaches with limited application to GGL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both approaches in GGL's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches with a justified decision covering prevention, cost and quality.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how GGL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $1,800,000 ÷ ($95 − $35) = $1,800,000 ÷ $60 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 guest visits a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $95 − $35 = $60. Answer: contribution per unit is $60.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways GGL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. GGL can compare the 30,000-visit break-even with 55,000 guest visits, a margin of safety of 25,000, to judge how far attendance can fall while the new dining floor opens.
2. The $60 contribution lets managers test the survey premium: if the 66% who would pay $8 more did so, contribution would be $68 and break-even $1,800,000 ÷ $68 = 26,471 visits, showing the value of cleanliness improvements.
3. Managers can use break-even to set the visitor volume needed to cover $1,800,000 fixed costs and service the $900,000 loan before expanding further.
4. Average total cost of $1,800,000 ÷ 55,000 + $35 = about $67.73 per visit can be benchmarked monthly to expose the 10.1% food-cost rise and direct the $320 waste-training spend.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 guest visits | (ii) Contribution per unit = $60 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 55,000 visits; $8 cleanliness premium and break-even of 26,471; loan-service target; and average total cost of $67.73 to track 10.1% food inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GGL's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has GGL's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.49 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.61 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $300,000 inventories + $200,000 trade receivables + $100,000 cash = $600,000; 2025 current assets = $360,000 + $170,000 + $80,000 = $610,000. Short-term cover 2024 = $600,000 ÷ $400,000 = 1.50; 2025 = $610,000 ÷ $410,000 = 1.49. Excluding stock, 2024 = ($600,000 − $300,000) ÷ $400,000 = $300,000 ÷ $400,000 = 0.75; 2025 = ($610,000 − $360,000) ÷ $410,000 = $250,000 ÷ $410,000 = 0.61.

Evaluation: Liquidity has deteriorated, especially on the stricter measure. Current assets rose only from $600,000 to $610,000 while current liabilities increased from $400,000 to $410,000, leaving short-term cover almost unchanged and slightly lower. More seriously, inventories grew from $300,000 to $360,000 and cash fell from $100,000 to $80,000, so the business holds more stock and less money; excluding that stock, near-term cover fell from 0.75 to 0.61. Trade receivables did fall from $200,000 to $170,000, which helps, but not enough to offset the weaker cash and higher liabilities while GGL plans to spend $1,500,000 and owes $900,000 on loan with only $80,000 in cash.

Conclusion: GGL's financial position has not improved. Both measures fell, and the sharper fall in the stricter ratio shows the business is more dependent on selling inventories to meet short-term debts. GGL should reduce stock and rebuild cash before drawing further on debt for the new floor.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, cash and liabilities and a justified conclusion on GGL's financial position.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GGL of introducing a waste-reduction programme in its food court.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey found 53% of 800 visitors consider waste reduction important and 66% would pay $8 more for a cleaner venue, so cutting the 7.8% food-waste rate can attract these guests and lift the $95 price or visitor numbers. Less waste also lowers the $35 variable cost per visit, protecting the $60 contribution against 10.1% food inflation; 13,500 visits last quarter show a large guest base to influence.

Disadvantage: Introducing recycling and training 120 staff costs $320 per employee and management time, adding to $1,800,000 fixed costs while a $900,000 loan is outstanding. The programme also needs monitoring to fall from 7.8% toward 5.2%, and if the new floor attracts more visits the absolute volume of waste may still rise, limiting the benefit to the $1,500,000 investment. With $1,800,000 fixed costs already high, payback may be slow, and if waste falls only gradually from 7.8% the 53% who value it may barely notice.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to GGL's survey, waste rate and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 10.1% rise in food and beverage input costs will affect GGL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If GGL's $900,000 loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.75% × $900,000 = $6,750 a year, which is small against $1,800,000 fixed costs; a fixed-rate loan would see no direct change. Higher rates may also make the $1,500,000 floor harder to finance and discourage the 2.9% growth in leisure spending, but fixing the rate limits this.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.12 per hour): With a workforce of 120, wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. No hours or individual pay are given, so a defensible annual wage total cannot be invented; the test is productivity — 55,000 guest visits ÷ 120 staff = about 458 visits per employee. If the new dining floor lifts visits, the extra pay is absorbed; if complaints and 7.8% waste persist, the $60 contribution per visit is squeezed.

Food and beverage costs (+10.1%): These feed the $35 variable cost per guest visit. As an illustrative upper bound, if the whole $35 rose 10.1% that is $3.54 per visit (10.1% × $35), or roughly $194,000 a year at 55,000 visits. Even a partial rise cuts the $60 contribution, and the $8 premium wanted by 66% of guests offsets only part of it, especially with only 2.9% leisure-spending growth.

Conclusion: The 10.1% rise in food and beverage costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every guest visit and directly erodes the $60 contribution that must cover $1,800,000 fixed costs and the $900,000 loan, whereas the interest rise is small and fixable and the wage effect depends on productivity from the new floor.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to GGL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GGL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in GGL's context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
